newsitem.title: FRANCE: Paris stocks seen falling hard on election results.
newsitem.headline: Paris stocks seen falling hard on election results.

text.p: The French bourse is expected to fall sharply on news that the Communists will hold the balance of power in a new French government after the Socialists failed to win an outright majority of parliamentary seats.

Traders and analysts predicted a selloff on Monday of three to four percent on the blue chip CAC-40 index, which lost 6.48 percent last week after the left's upset victory in the first round of the legislative election called by conservative President Jacques Chirac to strengthen his mandate.
Although investors had given up hope for a victory by the centre-right RPR-UDF coalition, brokers said the market had not priced in the prospect of Communists in the new government.
"With that outcome, you could look for a drop of three to four percent tomorrow," said Gary Dugan, equities strategist at JP Morgan.

The Interior Ministry's count at 1030 GMT showed the Socialists and their left allies other than the Communists could not win an outright majority of 289 seats. The Communists at that time had won 36 seats, more than expected.
Pascal Nigen, equities analyst at GAN, predicted the bourse could fall as much as three percent on Monday.
"But you have to put things into perspective," he said. "Part of the election result was priced into the market. (Socialist leader Lionel) Jospin has been making very moderate noises."
Nigen said he did not expect the Communists to be given important ministries.
But Elisabetta Castelli, head of international equities at CDC Bourse, said the knee-jerk reaction on the bourse would be painful and the CAC index could fall three percent on Monday.
"Communists in the government...would be met by suspicion from U.S. investors," she said.

Paribas economist Dominique Barbet said the bourse would react to the results more than other markets, as it did last week, because of the greater presence of foreign investors who account for about 40 percent.
Economist Patrick Mange at Deutsche Bank expects a fall of up to four percent.
"We could lose 50 to 100 points tomorrow," said Olivier Blitz, senior trader at IFF Bourse.
He said if the CAC broke through strong technical support at the 2,530 point level, it could fall to 2,450 points.
A survey of 10 brokerage firms conducted last Friday showed they expected the CAC to fall to between 2,380 and 2,525 in the near term if the left won the parliamentary election.

Brokers said the stockmarket will remain nervous until the new government outlined its programme. "There will be considerable volatility as announcements come through on policy decisions," Castelli said.
"Until we get an absolutely clear indication on France Telecom, I see privatisation stocks and restructuring stories continuing to underperform," said Dugan at JP Morgan.

He said the decision whether to go ahead with the partial privatisation of France Telecom -- scheduled by the outgoing government to begin in the coming week -- would be key "to judge how left-wing this government will be".
Jospin said he would consult with the staff but stressed recently that the decision would be made by the government.
The outlook for carmaker Renault, 46 percent state-owned, may also be clouded because its restructuring plans could be placed in doubt by the election results.
Jospin said he would ask Renault to look for ways to keep its doomed Belgian plant in Vilvoorde open. But to investors, the closure is symbolic of a much-needed restructuring.
Stocks in the banking, defence/aerospace and other sectors due for restructurings will also be vulnerable.
"The electorate is voting for full employment. It's going to be hard to achieve redundancy programmes in France," Dugan said.

"We'll have a bad day tomorrow," said Michelle Jardin at Credit Lyonnais Securities. But she said some shares look less exposed. "The sectors that perform best after victories by the left are consumer goods, retailers and exporters," Jardin said.
